# Tuberculosis- Learning about Experience with Nutritional Supplementation (TB LENS): Perspectives on a Nutritional Supplementation for Persons with TB and their Household Contacts

**Authors:** Madeline Carwile; Komal Jain; Madolyn Dauphinais; Chelsie Cintron; Janarthanan; Lindsey M. Locks; Kimberly Maloomian; Senbagavalli Prakash Babu; Nonika Rajkumari; R Manju; Prakash Babu Narasimhan; Lora Sabin; Pranay Sinha; Subitha Lakshminarayanan

**Affiliations:** 1. Boston Medical Center, Boston, MA, USA | 2. Department of Preventive and Social Medicine, Jawaharlal Institute of Postgraduate Medical Education and Research, Puducherry, India | 3. Department of Health Sciences, Boston University Sargent College of Health & Rehabilitation Sciences, Boston, MA, USA | 4. Department of Global Health, Boston University School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA | 5. Harvard Medical School (adjunct), Boston, MA, USA | 6. Kimba’s Kitchen, LLC, West Palm Beach, FL, USA | 7. MGMARI, Sri Balaji Vidyapeeth (Deemed to be University), Puducherry, India | 8. Section of Infectious Diseases, Department of Medicine, Boston University School of Medicine, Boston, MAs, USA

## Abstract

Undernutrition is a major driver of the tuberculosis (TB) epidemic, with one in five TB cases worldwide attributable to undernutrition. Nutritional interventions may reduce TB incidence and mortality for those at increased risk of developing TB. The TB LION (Tuberculosis - Learning the Impact Of Nutrition) study provides nutritional supplementation to household contacts (HHC) of TB index cases (n=60) to examine the impact of supplementation on progression from latent to active TB disease. TB LENS (Learning about Experience with Nutritional Supplementation), a qualitative sub-study of TB LION, was designed to examine attitudes and opinions regarding the provided nutritional supplementation to inform future interventions. We conducted in-depth interviews with HHCs from the TB LION study, local healthcare workers (HCWs) treating persons with TB, and with the two lead study nutritionists. Additionally, we held focus group discussions among HHCs and HCWs. We identified barriers and facilitators to intervention uptake and perspectives for future interventions. The results demonstrate the importance of culturally acceptable interventions with foods that participants enjoy eating and can prepare quickly. We also found an overwhelming preference for in-kind food delivery to the home over cash transfers. These results can inform future interventions to improve nutrition for households with TB.

## Introduction

Tuberculosis (TB) is the leading infectious cause of death worldwide, with 10.6 million new cases and 1.3 million deaths reported in 2022 (World Health Organization, 2023). Undernutrition, which blunts the immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is a leading risk factor for TB (Sinha et al., 2019). Indeed, one in five global TB cases are attributable to undernutrition (World Health Organization, 2023), and in India, which contributes more than a quarter of incident TB cases in the world annually, approximately 45% of all TB cases are attributable to undernutrition (Bhargava et al., 2022).

Recently, the Reducing Activation of Tuberculosis by Improvement of Nutrition Status (RATIONS) study demonstrated that providing nutritional support to household contacts (HHCs) of persons with TB (PWTB) in Jharkhand, India led to an approximate 40% reduction in incident TB and may also have reduced mortality among PWTB (Bhargava, Bhargava, Meher, Benedetti, et al., 2023; Bhargava, Bhargava, Meher, Teja, et al., 2023). These findings suggest the importance of implementation of nutritional support for households with TB. Moreover, a modeling study found that providing a 2600 kcal/day diet to undernourished Indians would be highly cost-effective in reducing TB incidence and mortality (Sinha et al., 2021).

To ensure that nutritional support interventions are successful, understanding the perspective of PWTB is critical. Many questions remain about the needs of households with TB, their preferences for different types of nutritional support, the barriers these households face in using provided support, and benefits outside of TB prevention. Qualitative research is needed to further our understanding of these questions.

Previous qualitative studies have highlighted the importance of social and nutritional support given the catastrophic costs and food insecurity caused by TB disease (Nirmal et al., 2022; Thiruvalluvan et al., 2017). Indeed, as antimycobacterial therapy eliminates the anorexia induced by TB disease, PWTB have frequently reported hunger and require nutritional support to continue treatment (Andom et al., 2023; Ayiraveetil et al., 2020; Munro et al., 2007). Food is an important determinant of adherence as many PWTB reported being unable to consume medications on an empty stomach, and left hospitals if food was not provided without charges (Munro et al., 2007). Recently, a qualitative study from India found that individuals receiving nutritional support perceived a faster resolution of their TB symptoms, while those who did not receive nutritional support felt that nutrition was an unmet need during treatment (Shah et al., 2024).

In a nutritional intervention study in Senegal, participants reported a preference for food baskets, as these were seen to improve food security more so than ready-to-use foods (Benzekri et al., 2019). A systematic review found that nutritional support, but not nutritional counseling alone, improves adherence to TB medications (Wagnew et al., 2024).

There is a paucity of qualitative studies that have examined barriers to the provision of nutritional interventions. One qualitative study of nutritional assessment, counseling, and support identified key barriers and facilitators at the organization, care provider, and PWTB levels. Barriers to implementation at the PWTB level include stigma and the tendency to share or sell provided ready-to-use foods (Degefa et al., 2021).

To expand knowledge on the experiences, perceptions, and preferences of South Indian households with TB receiving nutritional support, we conducted a qualitative study through the ongoing Tuberculosis - Learning the Impact of Nutrition (TB LION) study. This study’s objective was to understand the experience of receiving nutritional support and opportunities to optimize nutritional support programs for households with TB.

## Materials and methods

### Study setting and design

The TB LENS (Learning about Experience with Nutritional Supplementation) study enrolled participants across Puducherry, a city of approximately 1.2 million in South India, and two districts of the neighboring state of Tamil Nadu: Cuddalore (population ~ 2.6 million), and Villapuram (population ~ 3.5 million) (Cintron et al., 2021). Approximately 60% of TB disease in this region is attributable to undernutrition. Studies in the area have found that approximately 55% of PWTB and 28% of HHCs were underweight (Sinha et al., 2023; Sinha, Ezhumalai, et al., 2024). A study in 2019 found that household food insecurity in this region is 52.7% (95% CI 44.6%, 60.8%) (Kailasam et al., 2019). PWTB in India are at higher risk for food insecurity due to catastrophic costs associated with TB disease (Jeyashree et al., 2024; Kumar et al., 2020; Sinha et al., 2020).

In India, PWTB are eligible for free TB treatment in the public sector. TB treatment is not directly observed in-person. Under the “Nikshay Poshan Yojana,” the Indian government provides 500 rupees (5.75 USD) per month to PWTB, which they can use to purchase food (Nikshay Poshan Yojana [Nutritional Support to TB Patients], 2024), although concerns have been raised about the implementation of this program, such as delays in receipt of cash transfers, incomplete sums received, and inadequate quantity of funds (Jeyashree et al., 2024; Kumar et al., 2020). In November 2024, the monthly amount was increased to 1000 rupees (11.5 USD) per month. In addition, the recent “Nikshay Mitra” program connects donors to registered PWTB (Yadav, 2024).

TB LENS is a substudy of TB LION, an interventional study that aims to assess the impact of deworming and nutritional support on the immune response against TB for HHCs with evidence of latent infection (Cintron et al., 2021). The study purposively recruited household contacts who were malnourished and with intestinal parasitic infections and may not be representative of the broader population. All household contacts recruited into TB LION were between 18 and 60 years old, did not have diabetes, and lived with a person with microbiologically confirmed TB.

As part of this study, 60 undernourished (body mass index [BMI]<18.5 kg/m2) HHCs received rice (325 g/day), oil (5 g/day), lentils (117 g/day), and groundnuts (143 g/day) for six months. Food distributions were designed to fulfill the caloric, macronutrient, and micronutrient needs for all household members, and were developed based on guidance from the National TB Elimination Programme (Recommendations for Monthly Food Basket under PMTBMBA, n.d.). The TB LION food basket was developed using stakeholder input, focusing on affordable, locally available foods. The research team worked with a registered dietitian/licensed dietitian nutritionist (KM) and local study staff to ensure the food basket was nutritionally fulfilling and culturally appropriate. A pilot test was conducted by the research team to collect feedback on food preferences, acceptability, and delivery logistics. Each household received rations that provided adult participants with 2,600kCal/day and children under 14 years with 1,300kCal/day (Table 1). Participants received nutritional support within two months of the diagnosis of the index case in the household. Due to the large quantities provided and the distances traveled by HCWs, the study used a biweekly delivery mechanism. As such, raw ingredients were prioritized over prepared foods. HHCs were also provided with twice-daily micronutrient supplements (Life Extension Two-Per-Day multivitamin) throughout the six-month intervention period.

In TB LENS, we took a phenomenological approach. We conducted in-depth interviews (IDIs) and focus group discussions (FGDs) between June 2021-May 2023 with HHCs who received the TB LION nutritional intervention. The timing of the IDIs and FGDs varied, but was typically after completion of the six months of support. This allowed participants to reflect on the successes and challenges of the intervention as a whole. We also conducted IDIs and FGDs with healthcare workers (HCWs) and nutritionists engaged in providing nutritional support for PWTB. We discussed the delivery method and timing, quality and quantity of food provided, food preferences, and suggestions for the future.

### Study population

For TB LENS, we recruited household contacts who received the TB LION nutritional intervention using a convenience sampling approach, incorporating a purposive element to ensure gender balance between male and female subjects. Given TB LION’s visit structure, we prioritized enrollment among participants with upcoming visits to maximize efficiency and minimize burden on the subjects. Study staff approached and enrolled household contacts during TB LION study visits. No participants refused to participate or dropped out of the study, and each participant was interviewed once.

Similarly, we identified healthcare workers (HCWs) from TB clinics in Puducherry and Tamil Nadu, enrolling those who provided direct care to persons receiving nutritional supplementation under TB LION. After completing the FGDs, researchers conducted IDIs with the two principal nutritionists of the TB LION study.

The nutritionists played a key role in the study, delivering food to participants’ homes biweekly. During these visits, they monitored participants' weights, recorded the number of meals and snacks consumed each day, and documented any reasons for avoiding certain foods. They also provided nutritional counseling, educating participants on the role of nutrition in TB management, explaining the components of a balanced diet, and sharing healthy, culturally appropriate recipes. Through these efforts, the nutritionists served as key informants, offering valuable insights into the barriers, facilitators, and overall acceptability of the intervention.

A total of 26 in-depth interviews were conducted among 18 HHCs (twelve female and six male; see Table 2 for demographic information); six HCWs (four female and two male); and two TB LION nutritionists (both female). Three FGDs were also conducted: one with male HHCs; one with female HHCs; and one with HCWs.

### Data Collection

IDIs and FGDs were conducted by pairs of Tamil-speaking medical social workers, at least one of whom was the same sex as the participant(s).These medical social workers were trained in qualitative research by senior staff (PS, SL, and KJ). Interviewers had existing relationships with the study participants as part of the food delivery and health monitoring team, and participants knew minimal professional details about the study staff. Interview guides, including prompts, were used for both IDIs and FGDs.

IDIs with HHCs took place in their homes or in private rooms at nearby clinics. FGDs were held at JIPMER and at the Cuddalore District TB Centre. Field notes were made during the interviews, and they were referred to at the time of transcript preparation and analysis. IDIs and FGDs were audio-recorded for later transcription and translation into English by bilingual research assistants.

IDIs with the TB LION nutritionists were conducted by MC and were held following completion of all other IDIs and FGDs. For all of the IDIs and FGDs, no one else was present other than the researchers and study participants.

In-depth interviews lasted approximately one hour each, and focus group discussions ranged from one to three hours. The two FGDs with household contacts were separated by gender and included seven female and seven male participants, respectively. A single FGD was conducted with all eight health care workers.

All IDIs and FGDs followed a semi-structured approach, allowing for flexibility during the interviews (see Supplemental Material). The interview guide was developed using a quality improvement methodology, while the analysis was tailored to the acceptability framework for healthcare interventions (see Supplemental Tables). The main topics covered in all HHC IDIs included: overall opinions of the intervention, food quality and quantity, containers used to store the food, feedback on delivery methods, favorite and least-favorite foods of those provided, and suggestions for new foods to include in the future. More specific questions were covered by probes and sub-questions. IDIs with HCWs covered similar topics, but focused instead on personal opinions of the intervention and observations of subjects who received the intervention.

IDIs with the nutritionists were conducted using an adapted interview, with questions from the original interview guide modified based on information learned during analysis and team discussions. The goal of the nutritionist IDIs was to increase clarity on questions that arose from the HHC and HCW interviews regarding the nature of counselling, nature of food provision, acceptability in the field or apprehensions in receiving nutritional support.

FGDs covered similar topics to the IDIs, with a stronger focus on community-wide norms and perceptions rather than individual perspectives. The FGDs were structured to encourage further discussion that may not have occurred in the IDIs, particularly around barriers and suggestions for improvement, and to increase confidence in sharing opinions in a group setting.The research plan involved pre-determined numbers of IDIs and FGDs, and saturation was also achieved by the completion of data collection.

Notably, data were collected between June 2021 and May 2023, a period that overlapped with the COVID-19 pandemic and related lockdowns in India. While the interview guide included prompts related to this context, COVID-19 was not a primary focus of this analysis and did not emerge as a dominant theme. Instead, topics related to COVID-19 were covered in a separate analysis.

Extensive measures were taken to ensure validation of qualitative data that was collected during interviews. Rapport-building ensured participants felt comfortable sharing openly, while member checking at the end of the interviews allowed participants to confirm the accuracy of the interpretations. The transcripts were returned to participants for comments or correction after a week, and the study staff encouraged participants to share feedback on the findings. Triangulation of data sources was attempted by verifying findings with the field teams and using registers for data on utilization and adherence. Detailed descriptions of participant experiences and reflexivity helped contextualize the findings. Together, these steps reinforced the trustworthiness of the results.

### Data Analysis

All IDIs and FGDs were transcribed in Tamil then translated into English, apart from the nutritionist IDIs, which were conducted in English. IDI recordings were transcribed using Otter.ai and manual transcription. English language transcripts were analyzed using NVivo software (version 12) (Qualitative Data Analysis Software | NVivo, 2011). Coding was performed by one analyst (MC), who determined the frequency of findings associated with common themes and used a hybrid (inductive and deductive) methodology. The analyst identified direct statements that illustrated the key findings.

Initial parent codes were structured based on the acceptability framework for healthcare interventions using the primary structure of the IDI and FGD questions and themes. Child codes were identified during the coding process as primary themes were identified, with a content analysis focus, using an adapted acceptability framework. A codebook was generated by one author (MD) to maintain internal consistency (Supplemental Table 1). For HHCs, codes were identified using an overarching theme of acceptability, which included: subjects’ attitudes toward the intervention, their understanding and adherence to the intervention, costs associated with the intervention, willingness to participate, and their personal experiences during the course of the study. Themes for the HCWs followed a similar structure but included components that detailed both their personal opinions of the intervention and related outcomes, as well as further insights into the subjects’ acceptability, adherence, and coherence of the intervention. The study team reviewed the codebook to determine the key elements identified through the IDIs and FGDs and ensure agreement among team members (Figures 1 and 2).

### Ethics

The study was approved by the Institutional Review Boards of Boston University and Boston Medical Center (H-39980) and the JIPMER Institutional Ethics Committee. Participants provided written informed consent for IDIs and FGDs before data collection. HHCs were assured that their responses and decision to participate in the study would not affect their receipt of the nutritional intervention.

## Results

Our narrative synthesis of results is organized into three overarching themes: (1) impact of the nutritional intervention, (2) preferences regarding nutritional interventions, and (3) utilization of the intervention. These broad themes were derived from our underlying codebook (see Figures 1 and 2), which includes more granular subthemes. Table 3 provides illustrative quotations from participants and is structured according to the codebook categories. The text below highlights the most salient findings across these broader themes to enhance clarity and readability.

### Impact of nutritional intervention

Participants overwhelmingly expressed positive views about the nutritional intervention, indicating high overall acceptability. One woman (HHC-F-3) shared, “It was very helpful. I liked it very much. […] I wish I could have it for more than six months.” Reported benefits included self-perceived weight gain (89%), improved energy and mobility (50%), increased nutritional knowledge (50%), and reduced time spent acquiring food (39%). These themes were echoed in FGDs and nutritionist interviews, where participants were perceived to experience meaningful improvements in health and well-being.

For instance, a female HHC described how the intervention helped her mother regain independence: [The intervention] was very helpful. If you saw my mother, [she] couldnť even stand earlier, she used to struggle and stand with the support of her hands. But because we are giving her enough food using the supplies you have given, she is now very active and confident. Now, without any help from others she can manage to stand.(HHC-F-2)

Similarly, a male participant recounted health improvements in both his parents: When my mother used to have anemia earlier she didn’t eat well and she was not able to do any work and we had to help her. Now, after you gave the [intervention], she had gained weight and she is able to do all the work herself. My father also used to be very dull and had difficulty to go outside anywhere, but after [this intervention] he is able to walk better and he is able to go outside.(HHC-M-3)

Beyond health benefits, participants noted the convenience and economic relief of receiving food at home. As one woman explained: Since you have given the various food items at our doorstep, we didn’t have the travelling difficulties for buying those things, and we have saved so much money, so it was very useful and helpful for us.(HHC-F-10)

### Preferences regarding nutritional interventions

#### Perspectives on quality and quantity

Participants consistently praised the quality of the food provided. All HHC interviewees described the food as high quality, and 83% reported it was better than what they typically received from government-subsidized ration shops. As one nutritionist noted, “The feedback we got was always that the quality was good. They never complained about spoiled or damaged items.”

By contrast, opinions on food quantity varied. While 94% of HHCs stated that at least one item was provided in adequate quantity, 83% also reported that at least one item was given in excess. Groundnuts were the most frequently mentioned item as being over-supplied, although this varied by household. Meanwhile, oil was consistently cited as insufficient, with more than half of HHCs stating the oil provided did not meet their family’s needs, and many describing buying additional oil from the market.

One liter of oil, [should have been] 3 liters. For one family, 3 liters per month can be given. […] We need a little more oil because it is used daily. Dosa, idly, rice, all that requires oil. We need oil for all the meals so definitely it won’t be enough.

This was corroborated by both nutritionists, who observed that oil was used up quickly. One commented that the oil only lasted two or three days because, “in India, we are used to using more oil.”

Beyond oil, about one-third of HHCs mentioned that other items— such as pulses or grains— were also sometimes insufficient. Most HHC interviewees (83%) said they supplemented the provided foods with additional purchases such as vegetables, meat, and spices. In contrast, participants in the FGDs generally felt that the quantity was generous, though some noted the challenge of shared use within large households.

#### Perspectives on delivery methods and frequency

Most HHC interviewees (78%) preferred the existing home delivery model carried out by study staff. Participants valued the convenience of home delivery, noting that it saved time, kept food fresher, and allowed regular contact with the nutritionists. A majority also supported the biweekly frequency: only one participant suggested more frequent deliveries, while five suggested switching to a monthly schedule.

FGD participants and nutritionists echoed this preference. One nutritionist emphasized the feasibility and oversight biweekly delivery allowed: The frequency of 15 days is good only, we meet a lot of patients, then if we meet [once a week] that means there is no time. Nowadays in one day, we go to four members, four households, in the same day. So weekly once means we will not be able to go on with the participants. Monthly once is also good only, but we will not make sure that the participant is consuming or any other, [if] they sell or anything, we [wouldn’t] know.(N-1)

Participants were also asked about other delivery options, such as collecting food from ration shops, anganwadis, or clinics; receiving food from community health workers (CHWs); or using coupons or cash transfers. Most alternatives received mixed or negative feedback. For example, 72% of HHCs opposed coupons. Although some participants liked the idea of coupons, noting they were already purchasing additional food, most had concerns such as long queues, questions from store staff, and uncertainty about food quality. As one female participant (HHC-F-10) explained: “[to use] coupons we need to answer their questions and we need to be in a long queue. And also, we are unaware of the quality of the food items.”

Picking up food at the hospital or health clinic and delivery by community health workers were not the preferred strategies (only 39% and 6% approval, respectively). Interestingly, opposition for these delivery methods stemmed from mistrust. One female participant (HHC-F-2) explained that “[participants] cannot trust [HCWs]. They might take the food supplies provided by you. It is better if you deliver the food supplies to us.”

HCWs, in turn, expressed their own doubts about participant behavior. Some voiced concerns about potential misuse of the food, especially among persons with alcohol use disorders or limited literacy. One healthcare worker stated that participants “would have misused those given food items since you have been giving them in excess.” (HCW-F-2). Another healthcare workers stated that “some [participants] receive it happily… but a few think how to make money out of it. 80% understood iťs for their benefit. The other 20%— I doubt they’re using it properly.” (HCW-M-1)

Questions from neighbors were a common experience, with approximately half of HHCs reporting inquiries about the food delivery. Of these, 75% concealed the true purpose of the delivery. Reasons given to neighbors ranged from vague references to “weakness” or a sick child to fabricated relationships with study staff. For example: [The neighbors] have asked about why often some people are coming in the car to visit. Some asked why they are giving [us] these food items. […] I used to say, since we are unhealthier and lacking nutrition to government is providing us [food] to improve our health, for myself and my father.(HHC-F-4)

The nutritionists encouraged this, with one stating “We usually tell them [the recipients], say to the neighbor that we are your relatives— your child’s college mate, your child’s workmate.” (N-2).

While several HHC IDI participants anticipated that stigma would occur (such as neighbors treating them differently or gossiping behind their backs), instances of enacted stigma — actual differential treatment — were rare. Only three HHC IDI participants reported experiencing gossip, and no other examples of enacted stigma were mentioned. In the FGDs, two female participants reported experiencing stigma. Despite the low incidence of enacted stigma, privacy concerns were significant enough to influence delivery preferences, reinforcing the value of discreet, home-based approaches.

#### Cash transfers versus direct food provision

Most HHC interviewees (78%) and all HCWs expressed strong reservations about receiving cash in place of direct food provision. The dominant concern was that cash would be diverted toward other household expenses and not used for nutrition. As one female HHC explained: If given as money, the amount will be spent within 1 or 2 days. So, if given as groceries, it will be useful and right. If we get cash, people may spend it on buying other stuff and waste it. If [food supplies] are given everything would be fine.(HHC-F-2)

A male participant echoed this sentiment: Some expenses may come, so we will spend all the money. We are not able to safeguard the money at those times. So we can’t make use of the money in a proper way. Even we if get the food items, we will get it in lesser amount.(HHC-M-4)

Only three HHCs expressed openness to receiving cash— two preferred cash in hand, and one favored bank transfers. Similarly, FGD participants overwhelmingly opposed cash-based transfers. One woman summarized the prevailing view, stating that “all the money will be gone by spending [it] towards for some other expenses.”

Both nutritionists agreed that direct food provision was preferable. If cash had to be given, they recommended giving it to female heads of household, citing their better judgment and concern that male recipients might misuse it (e.g., on alcohol). One nutritionist (N-1) explained that the women would know “the needs of the household members” and would not “go to the shops and drink [alcohol].” If direct provision is not feasible, the nutritionists preferred coupons over cash or bank transfers.

#### Suggestions for improvements from HHCs

Despite repeated reassurances that their feedback would not affect their receipt of food or care, many HHC IDI participants were hesitant to suggest changes to the intervention. However, they were more forthcoming when asked about additional items they would like to see included in future food kits. Participants suggested a wide variety of foods, most commonly fruits (78%), vegetables (72%), nuts (61%), and eggs (44%). Foods recommended by participants are listed in table 4. These preferences were often framed in terms of taste, perceived nutritional benefit, and convenience. For instance, one male HHC participant (HHC-M-1) described how he would like to see flavored health supplements included in the intervention: Horlicks and glucose are essential. They are useful because in the morning we would feel like having coffee. If there is Horlicks, we can have that. If we are sweating or feel low on energy, we can dissolve glucose and have it. No need to go to the shop.

The FGD participants echoed many of the same suggestions, emphasizing vegetables, additional types of chickpeas and lentils, health mix (a locally available blend of grains, pulses, and nuts) or protein powder, and snack foods such as nuts and dried fruit.

Participants were also asked about their favorite and least favorite foods from the intervention. When asked about their favorite and least favorite items from the current food kit, participants’ responses varied widely. Several items, including green gram and groundnuts, were among both the most liked and most disliked foods. Notably, participants in both the IDIs and the FGDs described groundnuts and green gram as giving them digestive problems, such as constipation.

#### Suggestions for improvements from HCWs

HCWs were more open to sharing their views on ways to improve future interventions. Because HCWs were not direct beneficiaries of the food support but were closely involved in its delivery and monitoring, they were well-positioned to reflect on its overall acceptability and potential for scale-up. In IDIs, the HCWs suggested alternating food items to prevent boredom, providing recipes and nutritional education, and including prepared or store-bought snacks, such as groundnut cakes, spiced nuts, and instant noodles. During the FGDs, HCWs additionally proposed strategies for scaling up a future intervention, such as communication with nutritionists via WhatsApp, incorporating government and local leaders, and focusing on individuals with comorbid diabetes.

### Utilization of the intervention

During IDIs, HHCs described a range of food-related dynamics, including roles in meal preparation and daily eating patterns. Cooking responsibilities were almost exclusively borne by women, with only two participants mentioning male involvement in cooking. For example, one male participant shared that “Dad will be helpful in doing small things” (HHC-M-3) and the other that the father would cook only “if Mom is not there” (HHC-M-5).

IDI participants gave diverse answers when describing the location of their typical weekly meals. While eating at home was the most common response, participants also reported buying food at work, college, and restaurants. Similar sentiments were shared in the FGDs, with many male participants eating outside of the home due to the long workday. In the nutritionist IDIs, they posited eating outside of the house as one reason that participants were not gaining weight as they likely ate smaller quantites of poorly nutritious food: Moreover, we have the college-going girls, the college-going boys, they are not used to taking the food. They are not ready to take food and three meals in a home. […] They are going to the canteen, they will eat something there, so they are not ready to eat the food in the home.(N-2)

Perceptions of food monotony were mixed. Half of HHC IDI participants reported some boredom with the food, while 83% stated that they were not consistently bored— suggesting that monotony was often tied to specific items. One woman proposed varying preparation methods to avoid boredom, saying: “If we have the same thing daily, we will get bored. One day we should have it roasted, one day boiled […] If we have it like this, we won’t get bored” (HHC-F-1).

In the FGDs, male participants were more likely to mention food fatigue, with one noting that “Everything is good. But since we are eating it again and again repeatedly, it feels a little boring.”

In contrast, HCWs overwhelmingly believed that the limited variety of food would cause boredom among participants. This belief also affected their suggestions for improvement, as they suggested providing more types of food, alternating food between deliveries, or teaching new ways to prepare the food. Nutritionists were divided in their views— one noted no complaints of boredom, while the other described multiple instances of participants expressing fatigue with the provided items.

Regarding food use and sharing, all HHC IDI participants denied selling or sharing uncooked food, although two mentioned that they provided cooked food to family outside of their household, and one shared snacks with coworkers. The nutritionists similarly believed that the food was not being sold or widely redistributed. However, both raised the possibility that some households were stockpiling food in anticipation of the intervention’s conclusion at the end of six months. Notably, none of the HHCs reported keeping food for later.

The nutritionists viewed the intervention positively, noting that adherence was generally high. One stated: It works well, if the patients consume the food properly. […] Most of them consume. Some of them— the adolescent age, college-going and the [young] working people— they are not consuming properly due to their work nature [and] for studying college also, they are not eating properly.(N-1)

One hypothesized that lifestyle factors, such as late sleep and skipping breakfast, affected young participants’ weight gain. Nutritionists also noted occasional nonadherence driven by food fatigue or lack of variety, resulting in minimal weight gain.

Interestingly, there was some disagreement about whether body image concerns influenced adherence. One nutritionist did not believe participants were avoiding food due to a desire to stay slim, while another noted, “There were one or two participants like that. They want to be slim, so they do not want food” (N-2). These reflections suggest a complex interplay of age, lifestyle, and sociocultural factors in shaping nutritional behaviors.

## Discussion

The TB LENS study explored participants’ views on a comprehensive nutritional intervention and highlighted factors that could improve future nutritional interventions. Overall, the intervention was highly acceptable. Participants consistently reported improved physical activity and productivity— suggesting functional recovery may be a meaningful and underrecognized outcome of nutritional support. A key strength was the intervention’s completeness— the nutritional package was designed to fully meet participants’ caloric needs. By contrast, previous interventions (for persons with TB or HIV) that provided smaller supplementation have often seen no statistically significant results (Martins et al., 2009; Sudarsanam et al., 2011; Swaminathan et al., 2010). Additionally, by offsetting household expenditures on staples like rice and pulses, the intervention may have enabled recipients to diversify their diets, addressing persistent protein and micronutrient deficiencies through the purchase of vegetables, eggs, and meat.

Participants’ preferences offer important insights for tailoring future interventions to be both culturally acceptable and nutritionally relevant. There were varying preferences in terms of the composition of the intervention, with the only agreement being that the quantity of oil provided was insufficient. After receiving biweekly deliveries of food products, participants expressed limited enthusiasm for alternative delivery mechanisms such as centralized pickup, cash or voucher transfers, or distribution by community health workers. However, other studies have shown promise with these methods in other settings— for instance, a study among Indian women living with HIV demonstrated improved outcomes using a community health worker-delivered nutrition and education model (Nyamathi et al., 2019). These mixed findings underscore the importance of context-specific design and the value of formative qualitative research when planning delivery strategies.

One compelling finding was that both HHCs and HCWs were overwhelmingly opposed to cash transfers, suggesting that these funds would be used to pay other bills, rather than for food. Our findings resonate with those from a recent qualitative study nested within the RATIONS trial, which also identified preferences for in-kind food support over cash transfers, although views were not universally aligned and some participants of the RATIONS study expressed a need for both monetary and in-kind support (Bandewar et al., 2025). Studies in other areas of India have found mixed preferences for cash transfers vs. in-kind transfers (based on factors such as income and standard of living) (Das & Sethi, 2023), or significant preference for in-kind transfers (Satapathy et al., 2022).

We identified several factors that limited full utilization of the intervention: lifestyles that compel individuals to eat outside of the home, boredom with the same food ingredients, and tendency to stockpile food for use beyond the intervention period. Increasing the variety of food products would likely improve engagement with the intervention and could encourage participants to consume more. Participants consistently expressed a desire for greater variety and convenience, particularly for snack foods that could be consumed quickly or on the go. Such additions could enhance adherence and weight gain, potentially improving TB treatment outcomes for persons with TB and reducing disease progression among HHCs. While convenience was highly valued, future interventions should prioritize snack options that are minimally processed and nutritionally targeted to address key dietary gaps.

Findings from this study suggest that future interventions in the region could adopt the TB LION food basket as a foundation, with modifications such as increasing the amount of oil, diversifying lentils and spices, incorporating fruit and vegetables, and possibly including some ready-made snack foods. The recently proposed energy-dense nutritional supplement may meet the participants’ stated need for flavored health supplements (Kumar et al., 2025). Since regional food preferences vary widely, interventions in other areas of India and globally will need tailoring. Ideally, local preferences would be incorporated in future interventions, though programmatic feasibility may take precedence. Preliminary studies, surveys, and FGDs are necessary to inform interventions outside the Tamil Nadu region.

Despite fear of stigma from neighbors, participants still preferred home delivery, expressing concern that picking up food in public spaces may increase the likelihood of stigma. This aligns with prior findings from the same region, which found that enacted stigma was lower than anticipated stigma (Sabin et al., 2021). While at-home delivery was feasible in TB LION due to the small cohort size, scalability remains uncertain. Based on learned lessons from the rollout of Nikshay Poshan Yojana, there needs to be an emphasis on operational simplicity (Mohan et al., 2024). Despite added costs, home delivery is likely to be cost-effective (McQuaid et al., 2025; Sinha, Dauphinais, et al., 2024).

Our study does have limitations. The study had a limited sample size, particularly for the HCW IDIs. However, we believe the sample size for both HHC and HCWs was adequate for a qualitative, exploratory study as we reached interview saturation, as well as the planned number of interviews. Participation in the study involved frequent nutritional assessment and answering questions related to nutrition and diet. This may have affected participants’ dietary choices, outside of the direct effects of the nutritional intervention. Moreover, the Hawthorne effect could have been present, particularly as participants knew that their weight and quantity of food consumed would be measured. Lastly, the quantity of food delivered by the TB LION study, which provided enough nutritional support to meet the recommended dietary allowance for both macronutrients and micronutrients, is far larger than is feasible in programmatic sessions. However, this was necessary to avoid making a type II error in assessing the impact of nutritional interventions on immune responses.

Further, participants were chosen largely via convenience sampling instead of purposive sampling. HCWs include accredited social health activists and auxiliary nurse midwives involved in follow-up and treatment support for PWTB in India. Future studies could benefit from selecting HHCs and HCWs based on specific factors such as their level of engagement, barriers encountered, or insights into intervention delivery. We acknowledge that having TB LION study staff conduct the IDIs and FGDs may have introduced bias. However, interviewers took steps to reduce social desirability bias, including emphasizing that honest responses would not affect food delivery and normalizing food sharing as an expected behavior. FGDs may have provided a space for more open dialogue due to increased confidence while speaking as part of a group. Additionally, because of the comfort and familiarity with the subjects from their relationships formed in the parent study, we believe biases due to power dynamics were minimized.

Lastly, this study took place during the COVID-19 pandemic, which interrupted and delayed data collection. Although the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic was not the primary focus of this manuscript, COVID-19 related lockdowns may have influenced food insecurity and perceptions of the nutritional support. We have previously reported on the specific impacts of COVID-19 lockdowns on food security and household hardship in related populations, and those findings offer complementary insight into the vulnerabilities experienced by participants during this time (Carwile et al., 2025).

## Conclusions

In the wake of the RATIONS trial, there needs to be an urgency about implementing acceptable and effective nutritional support for households with TB. The role of nutrition as a key TB risk factor is gaining global attention, particularly with conflict, climate change, and pandemic threats like COVID-19 reversing progress on food security, particularly among key and vulnerable populations at risk of TB (Carwile et al., 2025; Clark et al., 2025; Sinha, Carwile, et al., 2021). The TB LENS study offers timely, actionable insights to inform such interventions. However, given the deeply personal and context-specific nature of food, scaling up these efforts will require further operational and implementation research, including health-economic evaluations, to ensure impact and sustainability.
